nodes.name: Implanted brain-computer interfaces
nodes.summary: Electrode arrays in the brain whose signals are decoded, increasingly by neural networks, to move cursors and robot arms or produce speech for paralyzed people. Fewer than a hundred people had high-channel implants by 2026.

efforts.who: John Donoghue and colleagues (Brown University, BrainGate)
efforts.note: The first person to control a cursor with a Utah array implant, Matt Nagle.

efforts.who: UCSF (Edward Chang) and Stanford (Francis Willett, Jaimie Henderson) groups
efforts.note: Speech neuroprostheses decoding about 60 to 80 words a minute.
Neuralink's first human implant was in January 2024; secondary reports put its total near 26 people by mid-2026.

nodes.name: Brain-computer interfaces at scale
nodes.summary: Implanted high-bandwidth brain interfaces in routine medical use, with tens of thousands of people restored to fluent communication or movement. Elective use by healthy people would come later, if at all.

forecast.note: Implant counts grew from a handful to a few dozen between 2023 and 2026, against Neuralink's 2024 talk of over 1,000 implants in 2026. Reaching tens of thousands needs pivotal trials, regulatory approval (likely late 2020s for the first devices), reimbursement and surgical capacity. Medical devices such as cochlear implants took about 15 to 20 years from approval to that scale, which points to the late 2030s.

nodes.name: Automated AI research
nodes.summary: AI systems that can do the work of top AI research engineers on their own, from running experiments to designing new methods, so AI progress itself speeds up. Labs openly aim for it, and it is the main mechanism in fast takeoff scenarios.

forecast.note: Coding agents already finish many-hour software tasks, and METR's task horizons doubled about every 4 to 7 months through 2026. Research needs month-long autonomy, judgment about which experiments matter, and high reliability; extrapolating horizons from about 12 hours in 2026 to about a work-month gives roughly 2027 to 2029, and I add a year or two for the reliability and taste gap. The AI 2027 scenario put a superhuman coder in 2027, and its authors' own median forecasts were later.

sources.title: Kwa et al. 2025 (METR), Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks
Epoch AI, Training compute of frontier AI models grows by 4-5x per year

nodes.name: Artificial general intelligence (transformative AI)
nodes.summary: AI that can do essentially any cognitive work a skilled human can do remotely, at similar or lower cost. It would transform the economy and science, and how to make it safe is one of the central open problems of the time.

efforts.who: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, xAI, Meta Superintelligence Labs
efforts.note: All state AGI or superintelligence as a goal; OpenAI presented GPT-6 Astra (September 2026) as the start of an "AGI era".

efforts.who: DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot, Zhipu and others

forecast.note: Frontier training compute has grown about 4 to 5 times a year (Epoch), reaching about 1e27 FLOP in 2026, and Epoch judged about 2e29 FLOP feasible by 2030, limited mainly by power. METR's task horizons doubled about every 4 to 7 months to around half a working day by 2026. If those trends hold, systems that handle month-long projects arrive around 2028 to 2030; the gap from there to broadly human-level work across messy, long-horizon and physical-world-adjacent jobs is the main uncertainty. Metaculus's strong-AGI question had a community median around 2030 to 2033 in 2025 to 2026 snapshots (down from the 2050s in 2020), while the 2023 survey of 2,778 AI researchers gave a 50% chance of human-level machine intelligence by 2047, a date that has moved earlier with each survey. I weight the trend extrapolations most and put the median at 2032, with a long tail if scaling slows when compute growth hits power and capital limits around 2030.

nodes.name: Nuclear power
nodes.summary: Fission reactors that boil water to drive turbines, first feeding a grid at Obninsk in 1954. About 440 reactors now supply roughly 9 percent of the world's electricity with almost no carbon emissions.

efforts.note: First electricity from fission, enough to light four bulbs (December 20, 1951).
First reactor to feed a power grid (5 MW), June 27, 1954.
First commercial-scale nuclear station, opened October 1956.
First full-scale US plant, a pressurized water reactor adapted from the naval program that powered USS Nautilus (1955). The PWR became the world's dominant design.
Builds more reactors than the rest of the world combined in the 2020s.

effort.note: Rides on the Manhattan Project (about 130,000 people, about $30 billion in 2025 dollars). Vogtle 3 and 4 in Georgia cost about $35 billion for two units and Hinkley Point C is estimated near 46 billion pounds, which is why cost, not physics, is the constraint in the West.

World Nuclear Association, Nuclear Power in the World Today

nodes.name: Small modular reactors and advanced fission
nodes.summary: Factory-built reactors under about 300 MW, meant to cut nuclear costs through series production rather than one-off megaprojects. A handful run in Russia and China; the first Western units are under construction.

efforts.note: Two 35 MWe KLT-40S reactors on a barge at Pevek, commercial since May 2020.
High-temperature gas-cooled pebble-bed reactor, commercial operation December 2023.
125 MWe land-based PWR at Changjiang, Hainan; commissioning in 2026.

efforts.who: Ontario Power Generation and GE Vernova Hitachi, BWRX-300 at Darlington
efforts.note: Construction license April 2025; first unit grid power expected 2029 to 2030, three more planned.

efforts.who: TerraPower Natrium (Kemmerer, Wyoming); X-energy with Dow; Kairos Power Hermes
efforts.note: Sodium-cooled, pebble-bed and molten-salt-cooled designs under construction or licensing.
First US SMR design certified (2023 for 50 MWe module, uprate approved 2025); the first planned plant (CFPP, Utah) was cancelled in 2023 over cost.

efforts.who: US DOE Reactor Pilot Program (Antares, Valar Atomics, Deployable Energy, Aalo)
efforts.note: Four test reactors reached criticality by July 2026 against a July 4 goal of three.
Selected by Great British Energy, Nuclear in June 2025.

sources.title: US DOE, Fourth criticality ahead of July 4th goal (2026)
World Nuclear News, Additional SMRs in the pipeline for Darlington

nodes.name: Thorium molten salt reactors
nodes.summary: Reactors with fuel dissolved in molten fluoride salt that can breed fissile uranium-233 from abundant thorium. Oak Ridge ran a test reactor in the 1960s; China's Wuwei reactor converted thorium to uranium in 2025.

efforts.who: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Molten Salt Reactor Experiment
efforts.note: Ran 1965 to 1969, including on U-233; program cut in favor of sodium fast breeders.

efforts.who: Shanghai Institute of Applied Physics (CAS), TMSR-LF1
efforts.note: 2 MWt; critical October 2023, thorium added October 2024, first thorium-to-uranium conversion announced November 2025. A 373 MWt follow-on is planned around 2030.

efforts.who: Copenhagen Atomics, Terrestrial Energy, Flibe Energy

efforts.note: Solid-fuel route through fast breeders rather than molten salt.

forecast.note: Read as a thorium-fueled molten salt reactor delivering grid power. China has moved fastest, from construction start (2018) to thorium conversion (2025) in seven years, and plans a 10 MWe class demo near 2030. Salt corrosion, tritium handling and fuel reprocessing are unsolved at commercial scale, and thorium is not needed while uranium is cheap, so Western efforts lag. Best guess mid-2030s in China, later elsewhere.

nodes.name: Laser
nodes.summary: A light source that amplifies light by stimulated emission into an intense, coherent beam, first built by Theodore Maiman with a ruby crystal in 1960. It underlies fiber optics, precision measurement, laser fusion and much of modern manufacturing.

efforts.note: The microwave precursor; Townes and Schawlow proposed the optical version in 1958.

efforts.who: Nikolay Basov and Alexander Prokhorov (Lebedev Institute)
efforts.note: Shared the 1964 Nobel with Townes.
First working laser, May 16, 1960.

sources.title: APS Physics History, Maiman builds first working laser

nodes.name: Tokamak magnetic confinement
nodes.summary: A doughnut-shaped magnetic bottle that holds plasma hot enough for fusion, proposed by Tamm and Sakharov in 1951. Soviet T-3 results in 1968 made it the world's main fusion approach.

efforts.note: Reported 10 million degree plasmas; a British Culham team confirmed with laser scattering in 1969.
Record 69 MJ of fusion energy in its final experiments before closing in December 2023.
1,066 seconds of high-confinement plasma, January 2025.
1,337 second plasma, February 2025.

efforts.who: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory stellarator program; Wendelstein 7-X (Max Planck)
efforts.note: Stellarators, the twisted alternative, revived by W7-X (first plasma 2015).

nodes.name: Laser fusion ignition
nodes.summary: On December 5, 2022, the National Ignition Facility got more fusion energy out of a fuel pellet (3.15 MJ) than its lasers put in (2.05 MJ), the first controlled fusion ignition. By 2025 shots reached 8.6 MJ, a target gain above 4.

efforts.who: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, National Ignition Facility
efforts.note: Gain counts laser energy at the target only; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid. Record 8.6 MJ from 2.08 MJ in April 2025.

effort.note: About $3.5 billion to build (finished 2009), plus over a decade of operation, mostly funded for weapons stewardship.

sources.title: Physics World, NIF laser fusion milestone ignites debate

nodes.name: Fusion power plant
nodes.summary: A power plant that makes net electricity by fusing hydrogen isotopes, with abundant fuel and no long-lived high-level waste. Science gain has been shown, but no device has yet made net electricity.

efforts.who: ITER (EU, China, India, Japan, Korea, Russia, USA)
efforts.note: 2024 baseline moved start of research operations to 2034 and deuterium-tritium to 2039, adding about 5 billion euros. Aims at Q=10, not electricity.
Ignition December 2022; laser drivers need roughly 100 times better wall-plug efficiency for a plant.

efforts.who: Commonwealth Fusion Systems, SPARC then ARC
efforts.note: High-field REBCO tokamak; 20 T magnet test 2021, SPARC first plasma targeted 2027, ARC plant in Virginia early 2030s.
Pulsed field-reversed configuration with direct energy recovery; broke ground on Orion in Malaga, Washington in 2025 for a 50 MW Microsoft contract by 2028.
Beam-driven FRC; announced a merger with Trump Media and Technology Group in December 2025 and plans a 50 MWe plant.
BEST, a compact superconducting tokamak aiming at burning plasma with Q above 1 (design Q=5), due end of 2027; CFEDR demo to follow.
Spherical tokamaks; STEP prototype plant at West Burton targeted 2040.

efforts.who: General Fusion, Zap Energy, Type One Energy, Proxima Fusion, Marvel Fusion, Pacific Fusion
Energy Singularity; China Fusion Energy Co.
efforts.note: Chinese private and state HTS tokamaks (HH70 first plasma 2024).

effort.note: ITER alone is officially over 20 billion euros plus the 2024 overrun; the US DOE once estimated the full in-kind total near $65 billion. Private fusion firms raised roughly $10 billion by 2025 (Fusion Industry Association). Public fusion research worldwide has run on the order of $1 to 2 billion a year since the 1970s.

forecast.note: Read as first fusion electricity sold to a grid from a plant with net electric gain. Company dates (Helion 2028, CFS early 2030s, TAE, STEP 2040) have a poor record: SPARC slipped from 2025 to 2027, ITER first plasma from 2016 to 2034, and Helion has missed earlier stated dates. Metaculus's 100 MW question sits near 2041 (quartiles about 2034 to 2055). The Fusion Industry Association survey says most firms expect grid power in the 2030s, but that is self-reported. Tritium breeding, materials under neutron flux and plant availability are untested. I put a first small net-electric plant late 2030s, meaningful share of world power after 2050.

nodes.name: Silicon solar cell
nodes.summary: A semiconductor junction that turns sunlight directly into electricity, first made practical at Bell Labs in 1954 at about 6 percent efficiency. Module prices fell over 99 percent since 1975, making it the cheapest new electricity in much of the world.

efforts.who: Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller, Gerald Pearson (Bell Labs)
efforts.note: Announced April 25, 1954.
First solar-powered satellite; space was PV's first real market.

efforts.who: Germany's feed-in tariff (EEG, 2000) and Chinese manufacturers (LONGi, Jinko, Trina, Tongwei)
efforts.note: German demand then Chinese scale drove the learning curve; China makes over 80 percent of the world's modules.

effort.note: Price fell about 20 percent per doubling of cumulative capacity (Wright's law), from about $132/W in 1975 to $0.27/W in 2024 (2025 dollars). The world added about 510 GW in 2025, past 2.4 TW cumulative. Silver paste is a constraint at terawatt scale; makers are shifting to copper metallization.

nodes.name: Perovskite solar cells
nodes.summary: Solar cells made from cheap, solution-processed metal halide perovskite crystals, first reported at 3.8 percent efficiency in 2009 and above 26 percent within 15 years. Their weakness is degradation under heat, light and moisture.

efforts.who: Akihiro Kojima, Tsutomu Miyasaka and colleagues (Toin University of Yokohama)
Henry Snaith (Oxford) and Nam-Gyu Park (Sungkyunkwan) groups
efforts.note: Solid-state cells near 10 percent launched the field.

nodes.name: Perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells
nodes.summary: A perovskite layer stacked on a silicon cell to harvest blue and red light separately, beating silicon's practical limit of about 27 percent. Lab cells reached 35.5 percent in 2026; durable mass production is the open problem.

efforts.note: Certified 35.5 percent cell (ESTI, July 2026); 31.4 percent tandem module.
First commercial tandem module shipments, September 2024, from Brandenburg.

efforts.who: Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin, KAUST, EPFL/CSEM, Fraunhofer ISE

efforts.note: Pilot lines; Qcells targeted mass production around 2026 to 2027.

nodes.name: Utility-scale wind turbines
nodes.summary: Three-bladed, upwind, grid-connected turbines on the Danish design, scaled from tens of kilowatts in the late 1970s to 15 MW machines today. Global capacity passed about 1,300 GW in 2025.

efforts.note: 200 kW three-bladed prototype that set the "Danish concept".
Small commercial turbines sold into the California wind rush of the early 1980s.
Large two-bladed government turbines that mostly failed; incremental Danish scaling won.
China added about 120 GW in 2025 alone and holds over half of world capacity.

effort.note: Direct-drive generators use neodymium-iron-boron magnets (roughly 600 kg of magnet per MW, about a third of it rare earths); geared designs with induction generators avoid them at some cost in maintenance.

nodes.name: Offshore wind
nodes.summary: Wind farms built at sea, where winds are stronger and steadier, starting with Vindeby in Denmark in 1991. Floating platforms now open deep water.

efforts.note: Eleven 450 kW turbines.
First floating wind farm.
China has about half of world offshore capacity.

nodes.name: Lithium-ion battery
nodes.summary: A rechargeable battery that shuttles lithium ions between a layered oxide cathode and a carbon anode, commercialized by Sony in 1991. Cell prices fell about 99 percent since then, enabling phones, laptops, electric cars and grid storage.

efforts.note: Lithium titanium disulfide cathode; metallic lithium anode was a fire risk.
Lithium cobalt oxide cathode, doubling voltage.
Carbon (petroleum coke) anode, the first safe practical cell.
First commercial cells, in a camcorder.

efforts.who: CATL, BYD, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, Samsung SDI, SK On
efforts.note: Demand passed 1 TWh a year in 2024; Chinese makers hold about three quarters of production.

effort.note: Whittingham, Goodenough and Yoshino shared the 2019 Chemistry Nobel. The graphite anode and the cobalt in early cathodes are supply risks; nickel- rich and cobalt-free chemistries (LFP) and sodium-ion substitute.

sources.title: Ziegler and Trancik 2021, Re-examining rates of lithium-ion battery technology improvement

nodes.name: Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode
nodes.summary: A lithium-ion cathode of iron phosphate, reported by Goodenough's group in 1997, that needs no cobalt or nickel and resists fire. Cheap and long-lived, it now powers nearly half of new electric cars and most grid batteries.

efforts.who: Akshaya Padhi, John Goodenough and colleagues (University of Texas)

efforts.note: Cell-to-pack designs closed the energy density gap.

nodes.name: Sodium-ion battery
nodes.summary: A battery chemistry like lithium-ion but using abundant sodium, trading some energy density for lower cost and good cold-weather performance. Chinese makers began putting it in cars in 2024 to 2026.

efforts.note: 175 Wh/kg cells; first mass-production car unveiled February 2026, 10,000 to 20,000 cars expected in 2026.
Prussian-blue sodium startup that shut down in 2025.

sources.title: CnEVPost, CATL sodium batteries begin deployment in production passenger vehicles

nodes.name: Solid-state batteries
nodes.summary: Batteries with a solid ceramic or sulfide electrolyte instead of a flammable liquid, allowing a lithium-metal anode for more energy and less fire risk. Prototype cells exist; making them cheaply at scale is the hurdle.

efforts.note: Sulfide electrolyte; production for EVs targeted 2027 to 2028. Toyota once aimed at the 2020 Olympics.
Anode-free ceramic separator; B-sample cells 2025, Eagle line 2026, license up to 80 GWh.

efforts.who: Samsung SDI with BMW and Solid Power

efforts.note: Semi-solid packs already ship (NIO 150 kWh); all-solid targets 2027 to 2030.

efforts.who: Factorial Energy with Mercedes-Benz and Stellantis
efforts.note: Road tests of a semi-solid pack in 2025.

forecast.note: Read as all-solid-state cells in a series-production car sold in volume (tens of thousands a year). Every major player now points to 2027 to 2028 for small runs, but these dates have slipped repeatedly (Toyota's from 2020, QuantumScape's from 2024). Liquid LFP and sodium keep getting cheaper, which raises the bar. Small runs late 2020s; mass market early 2030s.

sources.title: EEPower, Solid-state batteries race to mass production
Janek and Zeier 2016, A solid future for battery development, Nature Energy

nodes.name: Modern electric cars
nodes.summary: Highway-capable cars powered by lithium-ion packs, beginning with the Tesla Roadster in 2008. Sales passed 20 million in 2025, a quarter of new cars, led by China.

efforts.note: Lead-acid then NiMH; recalled and crushed by 2003.
Chinese firms made about 60 percent of EVs sold in 2025; EVs were nearly 55 percent of China's car sales.

effort.note: Most motors use rare-earth permanent magnets; induction and externally excited motors (Tesla, BMW, Renault) substitute.

sources.title: IEA, Global EV Outlook 2026, trends in electric cars

nodes.name: Grid-scale battery storage
nodes.summary: Large lithium-ion installations that store solar and wind power for hours and stabilize grid frequency, made economic by falling cell prices. South Australia's Hornsdale reserve in 2017 showed what they could do.

efforts.who: Tesla and Neoen, Hornsdale Power Reserve
efforts.note: 100 MW / 129 MWh, built in under 100 days.
Over 10 GW of batteries shifting solar into the evening peak.
Largest installer of new-type storage in the 2020s.

sources.title: IEA, Batteries and Secure Energy Transitions (2024)

nodes.name: Long-duration energy storage
nodes.summary: Storage that holds energy for days rather than hours, using flow batteries, iron-air cells, compressed air or heat, to cover windless, dark weeks on a renewable grid. Pumped hydro already does this where geography allows.

efforts.who: Dalian Rongke Power, vanadium flow battery
efforts.note: 100 MW / 400 MWh in Dalian.
100-hour batteries; first Great River Energy system now due 2027 after slipping from 2024.
Compressed air storage at hundreds of megawatts.
Thermal batteries for industrial heat.

sources.title: MIT Technology Review, Form Energy (2026 climate tech companies to watch)

nodes.name: Horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing
nodes.summary: Drilling sideways through shale and cracking it with pressurized water and sand to release trapped gas and oil. Proven in Texas's Barnett Shale around 1998, it made the US the world's largest oil and gas producer.

efforts.note: First experimental hydraulic fracture.

efforts.who: DOE Eastern Gas Shales Project and Gas Research Institute
efforts.note: Public research on shale, microseismic mapping and horizontal wells.
About 17 years of persistence in the Barnett before it paid.

efforts.who: Devon Energy and others, horizontal multistage wells

US EIA, Hydraulic fracturing accounts for most US oil and gas production

nodes.name: Green hydrogen from electrolysis
nodes.summary: Splitting water with renewable electricity to make hydrogen for steel, ammonia and fuels without fossil carbon. It works but costs two to four times hydrogen from natural gas, and many announced projects were cancelled in 2024 and 2025.

efforts.note: About 260 MW of electrolyzers, then the largest.

efforts.who: NEOM Green Hydrogen Company (ACWA Power, Air Products)
efforts.note: About 2.2 GW for ammonia export.
Hydrogen-reduced steel; hit funding trouble in 2025.

efforts.who: LONGi Hydrogen, Peric, thyssenkrupp nucera, Electric Hydrogen

nodes.name: Enhanced geothermal systems
nodes.summary: Making geothermal power almost anywhere by drilling into hot dry rock and fracturing it to circulate water, borrowing shale drilling methods. Fervo Energy's Cape Station in Utah delivered first utility-scale power in 2026.

efforts.who: Los Alamos, Fenton Hill hot dry rock project
efforts.note: Proved the concept but not the economics; ended 1995.
Small EGS plant, about 1.5 MW.

efforts.who: Fervo Energy, Project Red and Cape Station
efforts.note: Project Red on the grid in 2023; Cape Station first power September 2026, about 100 MW by early 2027 and 500 MW by 2028.

efforts.who: DOE Utah FORGE; Eavor (closed loop, Geretsried); Quaise Energy (millimeter-wave drilling); Sage Geosystems

sources.title: Fervo Energy, Cape Station first power (2026)

nodes.name: High-temperature superconductors
nodes.summary: Copper oxide ceramics that lose all electrical resistance at far higher temperatures than metals, found by Bednorz and Muller in 1986; YBCO works in cheap liquid nitrogen. REBCO tapes now enable compact fusion magnets.

efforts.who: Georg Bednorz and K. Alex Muller (IBM Zurich)
efforts.note: Lanthanum barium copper oxide at 35 K; Nobel 1987.

efforts.who: Maw-Kuen Wu and Paul Chu (Alabama, Houston)
efforts.note: YBCO at 93 K, above liquid nitrogen's 77 K.

efforts.who: Commonwealth Fusion Systems and MIT PSFC
efforts.note: 20 tesla large-bore REBCO fusion magnet.

efforts.who: Faraday Factory Japan, Shanghai Superconductor, SuperPower (Furukawa), Fujikura
efforts.note: REBCO tape makers scaling for fusion and cables.

effort.note: Older niobium superconductors need liquid helium at 4 K; HTS at 20 K or 77 K cuts helium demand, a real substitution since helium is scarce.

sources.title: MIT News, Tests show high-temperature superconducting magnets are ready for fusion

nodes.name: Room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductor
nodes.summary: A material that superconducts at everyday temperature and pressure, which would transform power lines, motors, magnets and computing. Hydrides come close only under crushing pressures, and recent claims (LK-99, Dias) collapsed.

efforts.who: Mikhail Eremets (Max Planck Mainz), hydrides H3S and LaH10
efforts.note: Superconductivity up to about 250 K, but at about 1.7 million atmospheres.
Room-temperature claims retracted from Nature in 2022 and 2023 after misconduct findings.
Viral claim; replications found copper sulfide impurities, not superconductivity.

efforts.who: Nickelate and materials-discovery AI efforts (Google DeepMind GNoME, Microsoft)

forecast.note: The record critical temperature at ambient pressure has been stuck near 133 to 138 K (mercury cuprates) since 1993. No theory rules out room temperature, but none predicts how to get it, and the field has a history of false claims. AI-guided materials search raises the search rate, not the odds per candidate. Low confidence; it may never happen.

sources.title: Drozdov et al. 2019, Superconductivity at 250 K in lanthanum hydride, Nature

nodes.name: Artificial satellites
nodes.summary: Objects placed in orbit around Earth, beginning with the Soviet Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957. Satellites now carry the world's navigation, weather forecasting, broadband and Earth imaging.

efforts.who: Sergei Korolev's OKB-1, Sputnik 1 on an R-7 missile
JPL and Army Ballistic Missile Agency, Explorer 1
efforts.note: Found the Van Allen radiation belts.

efforts.who: China (Dong Fang Hong 1, 1970), Japan (Ohsumi, 1970), France (Asterix, 1965), India (Rohini, 1980)

effort.note: Built on the R-7 ICBM program. By 2026 roughly 19,000 payloads were in orbit, over half of them Starlink.

sources.title: NASA, Sputnik and the origins of the Space Age

nodes.name: Communications satellites
nodes.summary: Satellites that relay telephone, television and data across oceans, first with Telstar in 1962 and from geostationary orbit by 1964, as Arthur C. Clarke had proposed in 1945. Intelsat made them a global utility.

efforts.who: Arthur C. Clarke, Extra-Terrestrial Relays (Wireless World)
efforts.note: Proposed three geostationary relays.

efforts.who: AT&T Bell Labs and NASA, Telstar 1

efforts.note: Syncom 3 broadcast the Tokyo Olympics from geostationary orbit.
Highly elliptical orbits to cover high latitudes.

sources.title: Communications satellite, Wikipedia (Clarke 1945 and early history)

nodes.name: Weather and Earth-observation satellites
nodes.summary: Satellites that image clouds, land, ice and oceans, from TIROS-1 in 1960 and Landsat in 1972 to daily whole-Earth imaging today. They made global weather forecasts and climate records possible.

efforts.note: First weather satellite images.
The longest continuous record of Earth's land surface; free data since 2008.

efforts.who: ESA Copernicus Sentinels; China Fengyun; Planet Labs
efforts.note: Planet's cubesat flock images the whole land surface daily.

nodes.name: Human spaceflight
nodes.summary: Sending people into space and returning them alive, first done by Yuri Gagarin on April 12, 1961. Russia, the US and China fly crews on their own rockets, and private companies now fly them too.

efforts.who: Alan Shepard (suborbital, May 1961), John Glenn (orbital, 1962), Project Mercury

efforts.note: First private company to fly astronauts to orbit, May 30, 2020.

sources.title: ESA, Yuri Gagarin, first man in space

nodes.name: Crewed Moon landing
nodes.summary: Apollo 11 landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Twelve people walked on the Moon in six landings through 1972, and no one has returned since.

efforts.who: NASA Apollo program (with North American, Grumman, Boeing, MIT Instrumentation Lab and others)

efforts.note: Four N1 launch failures 1969 to 1972; Luna 9 made the first soft landing (uncrewed) in 1966.

effort.note: $25.8 billion in then-year dollars, about $309 billion in 2025 dollars (Planetary Society, NASA New Start Index), peaking near 4 percent of the federal budget in 1966. The Apollo Guidance Computer was the largest early buyer of integrated circuits.

sources.title: Planetary Society, How much did the Apollo program cost?

nodes.name: Planetary probes
nodes.summary: Robotic spacecraft sent to other worlds, from Mariner 2 passing Venus in 1962 to Voyager leaving the solar system. Every planet, and Pluto, has now been visited.

efforts.note: First impact on the Moon and first images of its far side.
First soft landing on another planet.
Grand tour of the outer planets; Voyager 1 reached interstellar space in 2012.
Rosetta comet landing (2014), Mangalyaan (2014), Chang'e 4 far-side landing (2019).

nodes.name: Space stations
nodes.summary: Crewed outposts in orbit for long stays and research, starting with Salyut 1 in 1971. The International Space Station has been occupied without a break since November 2000, and China runs its own Tiangong.

efforts.who: International Space Station (NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, CSA)
efforts.note: To be deorbited around 2030.

efforts.who: Axiom Space, Vast (Haven-1), Starlab, Blue Origin Orbital Reef
efforts.note: Commercial successors to the ISS.

effort.note: The ISS is often cited at about $150 billion across partners, the most expensive single object ever built.

nodes.name: Space Shuttle
nodes.summary: NASA's partly reusable winged spacecraft, flown 135 times from 1981 to 2011. It built the ISS and launched Hubble, but refurbishment made it far more expensive per kilogram than promised, and two orbiters were lost with crews.

efforts.note: Challenger (1986) and Columbia (2003) disasters killed 14 astronauts.
One uncrewed orbital flight.

effort.note: About $209 billion in 2010 dollars over the program, roughly $1.5 billion per flight; CSIS puts it at about $65,400 per kg to LEO.

sources.title: Space.com, NASA's shuttle program cost $209 billion

nodes.name: Atomic clock
nodes.summary: A clock that counts the microwave frequency of a cesium atom's transition, first built by Louis Essen in 1955. Since 1967 the second has been defined this way, and satellite navigation depends on such clocks.

efforts.who: Louis Essen and Jack Parry (National Physical Laboratory)

efforts.note: Optical clocks 100 times more precise may redefine the second around 2030.

nodes.name: Global Positioning System
nodes.summary: A US military constellation of satellites with atomic clocks that lets any receiver compute its position to meters, first launched in 1978 and fully operational in 1995. Opened fully to civilians in 2000, it now times phone networks, power grids and finance as well as guiding people.

efforts.who: US Air Force NAVSTAR program (Bradford Parkinson and others)
efforts.note: First Block I satellite February 1978; full operational capability 1995; Selective Availability turned off May 2000.

effort.note: About $7.2 billion in R&D and procurement through 1994 in then-year dollars (roughly $15 to 20 billion today), and about $1.5 to 2 billion a year since. Relativity matters: uncorrected, clocks would drift about 38 microseconds a day, about 10 km of position error.

sources.title: National Academies, The Global Positioning System (1995), costs

nodes.name: Space telescopes
nodes.summary: Telescopes above the atmosphere, which blurs visible light and blocks infrared, X-rays and ultraviolet. Hubble (1990) and the James Webb Space Telescope (2021) changed what we know about the universe's age, expansion and first galaxies.

efforts.who: NASA and ESA, Hubble Space Telescope
efforts.note: Launched with a flawed mirror, fixed by astronauts in 1993.

efforts.who: NASA, ESA, CSA, James Webb Space Telescope
NASA Nancy Grace Roman; China's Xuntian

effort.note: Hubble cost about $1.5 billion at launch (about $16 billion over its life); JWST about $10 billion, from 1996 to 2021.

nodes.name: Exoplanet detection
nodes.summary: The discovery of planets around other stars, first around a normal Sun-like star (51 Pegasi b) by Mayor and Queloz in 1995. More than 6,000 are now confirmed, many by the Kepler and TESS space telescopes.

efforts.note: Planets around a pulsar.
Nobel 2019.

nodes.name: Fixed-price commercial space contracts (COTS)
nodes.summary: NASA's 2006 Commercial Orbital Transportation Services program paid companies fixed sums for milestones instead of owning rocket designs. It funded Falcon 9 and Dragon, and became the model for commercial crew and lunar landers.

efforts.who: NASA (Alan Lindenmoyer), SpaceX and Orbital Sciences
efforts.note: Dragon reached the ISS in May 2012.

effort.note: NASA paid about $800 million across COTS partners (then-year dollars).

sources.title: NASA, Commercial Orbital Transportation Services, a new era in spaceflight

nodes.name: Reusable orbital rocket boosters
nodes.summary: Rocket first stages that fly back and land upright to be reused, first done by a SpaceX Falcon 9 on December 21, 2015. Some boosters have flown more than 35 times, and SpaceX now launches most of the world's mass to orbit.

efforts.note: Suborbital vertical-landing test vehicle.

efforts.who: Blue Origin, New Shepard (suborbital) and New Glenn
efforts.note: New Shepard landed November 2015; New Glenn's orbital booster first landed November 13, 2025.
First landing December 2015; first reflight March 2017; booster B1067 flew its 37th mission in August 2026.

efforts.who: LandSpace (Zhuque-3), Space Pioneer, CALT (Long March 12A); Rocket Lab Neutron; ArianeGroup Themis

effort.note: SpaceX put Falcon 9 v1.0 development at about $300 million (2011), and reusability at roughly $1 billion more. A 2011 NASA cost model estimated $1.7 to 4 billion for the same rocket under NASA practices.

sources.title: NASA, Falcon 9 cost analysis with NAFCOM (2011)
Spaceflight Now, Falcon 9 booster's record-breaking 35th flight (2026)

nodes.name: Satellite internet megaconstellations
nodes.summary: Thousands of mass-produced satellites in low orbit that give broadband to anywhere on Earth through phased-array dishes. Starlink passed 11,000 satellites in orbit and about 10 million subscribers in 2026.

efforts.note: First batch May 2019; 10.3 million subscribers at March 2026 per SpaceX's IPO filing.

effort.note: Raises orbital debris and astronomy concerns; most satellites deorbit within about five years.

nodes.name: Mars rovers
nodes.summary: Wheeled robots exploring the Martian surface, from Sojourner in 1997 to Perseverance, which is caching samples for return. They found evidence of past liquid water and habitable lakes.

efforts.who: NASA JPL (Sojourner 1997, Spirit and Opportunity 2004, Curiosity 2012, Perseverance 2021)
efforts.note: Perseverance's Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet, April 2021.

efforts.who: CNSA Tianwen-3; NASA/ESA Mars Sample Return
efforts.note: China aims to return samples around 2031; the NASA plan faced cancellation over cost.

nodes.name: Asteroid sample return
nodes.summary: Spacecraft that collect rock from an asteroid and bring it to Earth, first done by Japan's Hayabusa in 2010. Hayabusa2 and OSIRIS-REx returned grams of pristine carbon-rich material with amino acids.

efforts.note: 121.6 grams returned.
Launched May 2025.

nodes.name: Asteroid deflection
nodes.summary: Changing an asteroid's path by hitting it with a spacecraft. NASA's DART struck Dimorphos in September 2022 and shortened its orbit by about 33 minutes, the first time humans moved a celestial body on purpose.

efforts.who: NASA and Johns Hopkins APL, DART

efforts.note: Arrives at Didymos in late 2026 to measure the result.

efforts.who: Vera C. Rubin Observatory; NASA NEO Surveyor
efforts.note: Finding the asteroids comes first.

nodes.name: Fully reusable super-heavy launch (Starship)
nodes.summary: A rocket whose booster and upper stage both return and refly, aiming to cut launch cost per kilogram another tenfold or more. SpaceX's Starship has caught boosters in the launch tower, but its ship has not yet been recovered and reflown.

efforts.note: First flight April 2023; first tower catch October 2024; V3 debut (Flight 12) May 22, 2026, reached its suborbital target despite engine losses. Orbital refueling not yet shown.

effort.note: Very rough; SpaceX said in 2023 it was spending about $2 billion a year on Starship. NASA's lunar lander contracts cover about $4 billion.

forecast.note: Read as a Starship ship recovered and reflown to orbit, with the booster also reused. Booster catches and reuse are done; the ship needs a working heat shield and catch. SpaceX tends to meet its technical goals 2 to 3 times later than Musk's stated dates (Falcon Heavy, crewed Dragon, Starship orbit). Musk's 2026 target suggests about 2028.

sources.title: TechCrunch, SpaceX wraps Starship V2 era

nodes.name: Return of people to the Moon
nodes.summary: Landing people on the Moon for the first time since 1972, this time near the south pole where ice may supply water and fuel. Artemis II flew four astronauts around the Moon in April 2026; the US and China both aim to land by about 2030.

efforts.who: NASA Artemis (SLS, Orion; SpaceX Starship HLS and Blue Origin Blue Moon landers)
efforts.note: Artemis II crewed flyby April 1 to 10, 2026. In 2026 NASA made Artemis III a 2027 Earth-orbit lander docking test and moved the first landing to Artemis IV, targeted 2028.
Abort and low-altitude rocket tests done in 2026; landing planned before 2030, then the ILRS base with Russia by 2035.

effort.note: NASA's Inspector General estimated Artemis at about $93 billion through 2025.

forecast.note: Read as any crewed landing. US landings depend on in-orbit propellant transfer with Starship or Blue Moon, not yet demonstrated, and Artemis dates have slipped from 2024 to 2028. China's program has met its milestones on schedule so far and targets before 2030, though its first uncrewed Long March 10 orbital flight is still ahead. Best guess 2029, by either.

sources.title: CSIS, Artemis rewritten, NASA's new Moon plan
Scientific American, How China could still win the new moon race
NASA OIG, NASA's management of the Artemis missions (2021)

nodes.name: People on Mars
nodes.summary: Landing a crew on Mars and bringing them home, a trip of about two to three years through deep-space radiation. It needs heavy lift, orbital refueling, propellant made from Martian air and reliable life support.

efforts.note: Musk long promised uncrewed Starships to Mars in the late-2026 window; reports in 2026 say that was shelved to focus on the Moon.
Officials have floated crewed missions in the 2030s.

forecast.note: Metaculus's question on the first human Mars landing had a median near 2035 to 2037 (quartiles about 2030 to 2046). I am later: orbital refueling, in-situ propellant and ship reentry are all undemonstrated, launch windows come every 26 months, and Musk's Mars dates have slipped by a window almost every cycle since 2016. Mid-2030s is possible if Starship matures quickly; early 2040s is my median.

sources.title: Metaculus, Date first human lands on Mars
Analytics Insight, SpaceX delays 2026 Mars mission

nodes.name: Permanent Mars settlement
nodes.summary: A permanently inhabited, growing settlement on Mars that could in time survive without supply ships from Earth. Beyond rockets, it needs closed-loop life support, local manufacturing, radiation shelter and an answer to whether people can raise children in 38 percent gravity.

efforts.note: Musk's stated goal of a self-sustaining city of a million people.

forecast.note: Read as a continuously inhabited base of at least about 100 people. The Antarctic analog took 50 years from first landing to permanent stations, with no rocket needed. Self-sufficiency is far harder: no closed ecological system (Biosphere 2) has run for years. Cheap launch is necessary, not sufficient. Very uncertain.

sources.title: Metaculus, Date first human lands on Mars
Weinersmith and Weinersmith, A City on Mars (2023)

nodes.name: Space-based solar power
nodes.summary: Large solar arrays in orbit that beam power to Earth as microwaves, catching sunlight around the clock. Proposed by Peter Glaser in 1968, it has only been shown in tiny demonstrations; launch cost is the deciding factor.

efforts.who: Caltech Space Solar Power Project, MAPLE
efforts.note: First wireless power beamed in space and detected on Earth, milliwatts.

efforts.who: JAXA and Japan Space Systems, OHISAMA
efforts.note: Small satellite to beam about 1 kW-class power to Usuda.
Plans MW-scale orbital demo in the 2030s.

forecast.note: Read as first MW-scale power delivered to a grid from orbit. NASA's 2024 Office of Technology, Policy and Strategy study found it costlier than ground renewables unless launch and in-space assembly costs fall dramatically. Starship-class launch could change that, but ground solar plus batteries keep getting cheaper too. China is the most likely first mover.

sources.title: Caltech, In a first, Caltech's space solar power demonstrator beams power to Earth
Glaser 1968, Power from the Sun, its future, Science

nodes.name: Asteroid mining
nodes.summary: Extracting water, metals or platinum-group elements from asteroids, most likely first as water for rocket fuel in space rather than metal shipped to Earth. Sample-return missions show the access, not the economics.

efforts.note: Both well-funded startups were sold off in 2018 to 2019 without mining.
Odin flyby probe lost contact after launch in February 2025.

forecast.note: Read as first commercial sale of material mined from an asteroid. Two earlier waves of startups failed for lack of buyers; in-space customers (depots, stations) do not yet exist, and shipping metal to Earth would crash its price. Depends on cheap launch and a space economy that needs local water.

sources.title: The Space Review, What happened to asteroid mining?

nodes.name: In-space manufacturing
nodes.summary: Making products in orbit that benefit from microgravity, such as pure drug crystals, optical fiber and semiconductor crystals, and returning them to Earth. Varda Space returned the first commercially made drug crystals in 2024.

efforts.note: W-1 crystallized ritonavir and landed in Utah, February 2024.

efforts.who: ISS National Lab, Redwire, Flawless Photonics
efforts.note: ZBLAN optical fiber drawn in orbit.

nodes.name: Probe to another star
nodes.summary: A spacecraft sent to reach another star system within a human lifetime, for example gram-scale light sails pushed to a fifth of light speed by ground-based lasers. Voyager 1, the fastest-leaving probe, would take about 75,000 years to reach the nearest star.

efforts.note: $100 million research program; work largely paused after 2022.

efforts.who: Johns Hopkins APL, Interstellar Probe concept
efforts.note: Heliopause probe, not a star mission.

forecast.note: Read as launching a probe designed to reach another star within a century. Laser sails need gigawatt-class phased lasers and materials that survive thousands of g; nothing is funded at that scale. Pure judgment.

nodes.name: Standard Model of particle physics
nodes.summary: The theory of the known elementary particles and three of the four forces, assembled from electroweak unification (1967) and quantum chromodynamics (1973). Every collider test since has agreed with it, though it leaves out gravity and dark matter.

efforts.who: Sheldon Glashow, Steven Weinberg, Abdus Salam
efforts.note: Electroweak theory; Nobel 1979.

efforts.who: David Gross, Frank Wilczek, David Politzer
efforts.note: Asymptotic freedom in QCD; Nobel 2004.

efforts.who: CERN (W and Z bosons, 1983), Fermilab (top quark, 1995)

nodes.name: Higgs boson discovery
nodes.summary: The particle that confirms how other particles get mass, predicted in 1964 and found at CERN's Large Hadron Collider on July 4, 2012. It completed the Standard Model.

efforts.note: Peter Higgs and Francois Englert shared the 2013 Nobel.

efforts.who: CERN Future Circular Collider; China CEPC
efforts.note: Proposed Higgs factories of about 15 billion Swiss francs.

effort.note: The LHC machine cost about 4.6 billion Swiss francs to build; ATLAS and CMS each have about 3,000 to 5,000 members.

nodes.name: Gravitational-wave detection
nodes.summary: Measuring ripples in spacetime from colliding black holes with laser interferometers 4 km long, sensitive to a thousandth of a proton's width. LIGO made the first detection on September 14, 2015, a century after Einstein's prediction.

efforts.who: LIGO (Caltech, MIT; Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne, Barry Barish)
efforts.note: Nobel 2017.
Space-based detector.

effort.note: NSF's largest single investment, about $1.1 billion over four decades.

nodes.name: Plate tectonics
nodes.summary: The theory that Earth's surface is made of moving plates that spread at ocean ridges and sink at trenches, settled by seafloor magnetic stripes between 1962 and 1968. It explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountains and where ores and oil form.

efforts.who: Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews (Cambridge); Lawrence Morley
efforts.note: Magnetic stripes on the seafloor, mapped with Navy magnetometers.

efforts.who: J. Tuzo Wilson, Dan McKenzie, Jason Morgan, Xavier Le Pichon

effort.note: Built on Alfred Wegener's rejected continental drift (1912) and Cold War ocean surveys and seismograph networks set up to detect nuclear tests.

sources.title: USGS, This Dynamic Earth, developing the theory

nodes.name: Modern climate science
nodes.summary: Measurements and models showing that carbon dioxide from fossil fuels is accumulating and warming Earth, from the Keeling curve (1958) to Manabe and Wetherald's 1967 model. Its predictions of about 3 degrees C per doubling of CO2 have held up.

efforts.who: Charles David Keeling (Scripps), Mauna Loa CO2 record

efforts.note: Manabe shared the 2021 Nobel.
Estimated 1.5 to 4.5 C of warming per CO2 doubling.

nodes.name: Scanning tunneling microscope
nodes.summary: A microscope that images individual atoms by measuring the quantum tunneling current to a sharp tip, built at IBM Zurich in 1981. In 1989 IBM used one to spell its name in 35 xenon atoms.

efforts.who: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer (IBM Zurich)
efforts.note: Nobel 1986; the atomic force microscope followed in 1986.
Positioned single atoms.

nodes.name: Jet airliner
nodes.summary: Passenger aircraft powered by jet engines, starting with the de Havilland Comet in 1952 and the Boeing 707 in 1958. Jets made intercontinental travel routine; airlines carried about 5 billion passengers in 2025.

efforts.note: Grounded after 1954 crashes from metal fatigue around square windows; the lessons reshaped aircraft design.
Wide-bodies and high-bypass turbofans cut cost per seat.

nodes.name: Supersonic airliner
nodes.summary: Concorde flew passengers at twice the speed of sound from 1976 to 2003, but noise, fuel cost and a 2000 crash ended it, and no one flies supersonic passengers today. Quieter designs are being tested to revive the idea.

efforts.who: BAC and Aerospatiale (Air France, British Airways)

efforts.note: Passenger service lasted 55 flights.

efforts.who: Boom Supersonic (XB-1 broke the sound barrier January 2025); NASA and Lockheed X-59 low-boom demonstrator (first flight October 2025)

effort.note: Development cost about 1.3 billion pounds by 1976, several times the 1962 estimate, all paid by the two governments.

nodes.lost: Retired October 24, 2003 after the Air France crash (2000) and the post-2001 travel slump; only 14 aircraft ever flew in service. Overland supersonic flight is banned in the US since 1973 because of sonic booms.

sources.title: AIAA, NASA's X-59 performs first flight

nodes.name: Container shipping
nodes.summary: Moving goods in standard steel boxes that transfer unopened between ships, trains and trucks, launched by Malcom McLean's Ideal X in 1956. It cut port labor and loading costs by over 90 percent and made global supply chains possible.

efforts.note: 58 containers, Newark to Houston, April 26, 1956.
The largest ships now carry about 24,000 twenty-foot boxes.

sources.title: Bernhofen, El-Sahli and Kneller 2016, Estimating the effects of the container revolution on world trade

nodes.name: High-speed rail
nodes.summary: Electric trains on dedicated track running at 200 to 350 km/h, starting with Japan's Tokaido Shinkansen on October 1, 1964. China built about 50,000 km by 2025, over two thirds of the world's network.

efforts.who: Japanese National Railways, Tokaido Shinkansen (Hideo Shima)
efforts.note: No passenger deaths from train accidents in over 60 years.
4.28 billion high-speed trips in 2025.

efforts.who: Shanghai Transrapid maglev (2004); JR Central Chuo Shinkansen maglev
efforts.note: The Chuo line, 500 km/h, is delayed to the mid-2030s or later.

nodes.name: Electric air taxis (eVTOL)
nodes.summary: Small battery-powered aircraft that take off and land vertically on many rotors, aimed at short city hops. China certified the first for commercial passenger operations in 2025; Western makers are in final certification.

efforts.note: Type certificate 2023, operating certificate for passenger flights March 2025.

efforts.who: Joby Aviation; Archer Aviation; Beta Technologies
efforts.note: Joby in the final stage of FAA type certification in 2026; Dubai launch planned.
Lilium shut down in 2025; Volocopter went insolvent and was sold.

nodes.name: Carbon fiber composites
nodes.summary: Fibers of nearly pure carbon, made by baking acrylic (PAN) filaments, set in epoxy to give parts stronger than steel at a fifth of the weight. Developed in Japan and Britain in the early 1960s, they now make up half of a Boeing 787.

efforts.note: High-performance graphite whiskers.

efforts.who: Akio Shindo (Osaka Government Industrial Research Institute)
efforts.note: PAN-based carbon fiber.

efforts.who: William Watt, Leslie Phillips, William Johnson (Royal Aircraft Establishment)

nodes.name: Synthetic diamond
nodes.summary: Diamond made from graphite at high pressure and temperature, first reproducibly at General Electric in 1954, later grown from gas by vapor deposition. Synthetic grit cuts and drills most of the world's hard materials.

efforts.note: Made diamonds but did not publish.

efforts.who: Chemical vapor deposition (Soviet and Japanese groups, 1970s to 1980s); Henan and Indian growers
efforts.note: Lab-grown gems passed half of US engagement rings in the 2020s.

nodes.name: Graphene
nodes.summary: A single layer of carbon atoms in a honeycomb, isolated with sticky tape by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov in 2004. It is the strongest, most conductive thin material known, though mass-market uses are still mostly additives and coatings.

efforts.who: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov (University of Manchester)
efforts.note: Nobel 2010.
About 1 billion euros over ten years.
Superconductivity at a "magic angle".

nodes.name: Carbon nanotubes and fullerenes
nodes.summary: Hollow molecules of pure carbon: soccer-ball fullerenes found in 1985 and the tubes Sumio Iijima imaged in 1991. They are used to strengthen materials and in battery electrodes, but never became the wonder cables once hoped.

efforts.who: Harold Kroto, Robert Curl, Richard Smalley (Rice), fullerenes
efforts.note: Nobel in Chemistry 1996.

efforts.who: Iijima and Ichihashi; Donald Bethune (IBM), single-wall tubes

sources.title: Iijima 1991, Helical microtubules of graphitic carbon, Nature

nodes.name: 3D printing (additive manufacturing)
nodes.summary: Building objects layer by layer from a digital model, first with stereolithography in the 1980s and now in plastic, metal, concrete and cells. It turned prototyping into a desktop task and makes rocket engines and implants that could not be machined.

efforts.who: Hideo Kodama (Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute)
efforts.note: Published photopolymer layering but let the patent lapse.
Patent filed 1984, granted 1986.

efforts.who: Carl Deckard and Joe Beaman (UT Austin), selective laser sintering; Scott Crump (Stratasys), fused deposition

efforts.note: Open-source self-copying printers; cheap printers spread after FDM patents expired in 2009.

efforts.who: SpaceX, Relativity, GE Aerospace (LEAP fuel nozzles), Rocket Lab
efforts.note: Printed metal engine parts in flight.

nodes.name: Molecular nanotechnology
nodes.summary: Building things atom by atom with programmable molecular machines, as Richard Feynman suggested in 1959 and Eric Drexler argued in 1986. Today's partial steps are DNA origami, molecular motors and designed proteins.

efforts.who: Richard Feynman, There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom
efforts.note: The founding lecture.

efforts.who: Eric Drexler, Engines of Creation (1986) and Nanosystems (1992)
efforts.note: Disputed by Richard Smalley in 2003 over "fat fingers" and "sticky fingers".

efforts.who: Ben Feringa, Fraser Stoddart, Jean-Pierre Sauvage
efforts.note: Nobel for molecular machines.

efforts.who: David Baker (UW Institute for Protein Design); UK ARIA programmable matter
efforts.note: AI-designed proteins as nanoscale parts.

forecast.note: Read as general-purpose machines that position atoms to build macroscopic products. Progress runs through biology (designed proteins, DNA nanostructures) rather than Drexler's diamond mechanosynthesis, which has had little experimental work. AI protein design (2024 Nobel) speeds parts design, not assembly. Pure judgment; the range is very wide.

sources.title: Chemical and Engineering News, Drexler and Smalley debate (2003)
Feynman 1959, There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom

nodes.name: Reverse-osmosis desalination
nodes.summary: Pushing seawater through membranes that pass water but not salt, made practical by Loeb and Sourirajan's membrane around 1960. About 95 million cubic meters a day are now desalinated, supplying most drinking water in Israel and the Gulf.

efforts.note: Asymmetric cellulose acetate membrane; first commercial RO plant at Coalinga, California in 1965.
Thermal desalination, still common where fuel is cheap.

efforts.who: John Cadotte (FilmTec), thin-film composite polyamide membrane
IDE Technologies (Sorek, 2013); ACWA Power; Saudi Water Authority
efforts.note: Seawater RO now takes about 3 kWh per cubic meter.

nodes.name: Carbon capture and storage
nodes.summary: Capturing CO2 from gas processing, power plants or factories and burying it deep underground. Norway's Sleipner has stored about a million metric tons a year since 1996, but global capture is only about 50 million metric tons a year, a tiny fraction of emissions.

efforts.note: CO2 injected to push out more oil, not for climate.
Driven by Norway's 1991 carbon tax.
First power plant CCS; below design capture rate.
First cross-border CO2 shipping and storage service.

sources.title: Global CCS Institute, Global Status of CCS 2024

nodes.name: Direct air capture
nodes.summary: Machines that pull CO2 straight out of the air with sorbents or solvents so it can be buried, proposed by Klaus Lackner in 1999. Plants exist but capture thousands, not millions, of tons and cost several hundred dollars a ton.

efforts.note: Mammoth's nameplate is 36,000 t a year, but it removed only 675 net tons in the first half of 2026.
Designed for 500,000 t a year; Phase 1 commissioning hit a delay in mid-2026.

effort.note: Stratos alone cost about $1.3 billion. Frontier's buyers (Stripe, Google, Shopify and others) pledged $1 billion in advance purchases from 2022.

sources.title: Gasworld, Climeworks upgrades DAC at Iceland facility after low capture
RBN Energy, Stratos DAC project targets Q2 2026 startup

nodes.name: Gigaton-scale carbon removal
nodes.summary: Removing a billion metric tons or more of CO2 a year with engineered methods such as direct air capture, bioenergy with capture, enhanced weathering and biochar. Climate pathways call for 7 to 9 billion metric tons a year of total removal by 2050; novel methods remove about 1.3 million today.

efforts.who: Frontier advance market commitment (Stripe, Alphabet, Shopify, Meta, McKinsey)

efforts.note: Largest single buyer, tens of millions of tons contracted, mostly BECCS and forestry.

efforts.who: US DAC hubs (DOE); EU Carbon Removal Certification

forecast.note: Read as 1 Gt a year of durable novel removal. From 1.3 Mt (2024) that is a roughly 770-fold scale-up. Solar took about 20 years to grow that much at 30 to 40 percent a year, but solar sells a product people want; removal only sells if policy pays for it. Plants are underperforming nameplate (Mammoth). If carbon prices or mandates arrive in the 2030s, mid-2050s is plausible; otherwise much later.

The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 2nd edition (2024)

nodes.name: Solar geoengineering
nodes.summary: Cooling the planet by reflecting a little sunlight, most plausibly with aerosols sprayed into the stratosphere the way the 1991 Pinatubo eruption cooled Earth by about half a degree. It would be cheap and fast but would not remove CO2, and its governance is unresolved.

efforts.note: Balloon test cancelled after opposition in Sweden.

efforts.who: UK ARIA Exploring Climate Cooling program
efforts.note: About 57 million pounds, including small outdoor experiments.
Startups; Mexico banned solar geoengineering experiments in 2023.

forecast.note: Read as deliberate deployment large enough to change global temperature. Technically feasible within about a decade of a decision (Smith and Wagner estimated about $2 billion a year for the first years). The barrier is political: a single country could act, which makes timing depend on climate damage and governance. Very uncertain.

sources.title: Smith and Wagner 2018, Stratospheric aerosol injection tactics and costs, Environmental Research Letters

nodes.name: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer at global scale
nodes.summary: The postwar spread of Haber-Bosch ammonia plants, many converted from explosives factories, that took nitrogen fertilizer from about 11 million tons a year in 1961 to over 100 million. Roughly half the world's people are fed by it.

efforts.who: US wartime ammonia plants converted to fertilizer
Yara, CF Industries, Sinopec and Chinese coal-based plants, Nutrien
efforts.note: About 1 to 2 percent of world energy goes into ammonia.

effort.note: Erisman et al. (2008) estimate about 48 percent of humanity depends on synthetic nitrogen. Green ammonia from electrolysis is the main substitute for gas feedstock.

sources.title: Erisman et al. 2008, How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world, Nature Geoscience

nodes.name: Center-pivot irrigation
nodes.summary: A long sprinkler arm that rotates around a well, watering a circle of up to a square kilometer, invented by Nebraska farmer Frank Zybach. It turned semi-arid plains into cropland and made the green circles seen from planes.

efforts.note: Patented 1952; Valmont and Lindsay industrialized it.

effort.note: Draws down aquifers such as the Ogallala faster than they recharge.

sources.title: Smithsonian, How center-pivot irrigation changed the landscape

nodes.name: Drip irrigation
nodes.summary: Delivering water drop by drop to each plant's roots through plastic tubes and emitters, using far less water than flooding or sprinklers. Simcha Blass and Kibbutz Hatzerim commercialized it as Netafim in 1965.

nodes.name: Precision agriculture
nodes.summary: Farming field by field and meter by meter with GPS-steered tractors, yield maps, soil sensors and variable-rate seeding and spraying. It saves seed, fertilizer and fuel and is now standard on large farms.

efforts.note: Yield monitors (1992) and GPS autosteer (late 1990s to 2000s).

efforts.who: Blue River Technology (Deere, See and Spray)
efforts.note: Camera-guided spot spraying of weeds.

sources.title: USDA ERS, Precision agriculture in the digital era (2023)

nodes.name: Cultivated meat
nodes.summary: Growing animal muscle and fat cells in bioreactors instead of raising animals. Singapore first approved sales in 2020 and the US in 2023, but costs and scale remain far from conventional meat, and several US states have banned it.

efforts.who: Mark Post (Maastricht University), first cultured burger
efforts.note: Cost about $330,000.

efforts.who: UPSIDE Foods; Mosa Meat; Aleph Farms; Vow
efforts.note: Florida and Alabama banned sales in 2024.

sources.title: GFI, State of the industry, cultivated meat

nodes.name: Federal research grants and the research university
nodes.summary: Governments paying universities, through competitive peer-reviewed grants, to do basic research and train scientists, as Vannevar Bush proposed in 1945. The model created the modern research university and was copied worldwide.

efforts.who: Vannevar Bush, Science, the Endless Frontier
efforts.note: Report to President Truman, July 1945, after the wartime OSRD.

efforts.who: NIH extramural grants (1946), Office of Naval Research (1946), National Science Foundation (1950)

efforts.note: Let universities patent federally funded inventions, spurring tech transfer.

efforts.who: Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, UK Research Councils, Japan JSPS, China NSFC (1986), European Research Council (2007)

effort.note: US federal R&D runs about $200 billion a year; world R&D spending passed about $2.5 trillion. Grant writing and administration take a large share of researchers' time; a 2007 US survey put administrative work at about 42 percent.

sources.title: NSF, National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics

nodes.name: DARPA model of research funding
nodes.summary: A small agency of temporary program managers with broad freedom to fund risky projects toward specific goals, founded as ARPA in 1958 after Sputnik. It seeded the internet, GPS receivers, stealth and self-driving cars, and has been copied as ARPA-E, ARPA-H and the UK's ARIA.

efforts.who: ARPA-E (2009), IARPA (2006), ARPA-H (2022), UK ARIA (2023), Germany SPRIND (2019)

efforts.note: Time-limited nonprofit teams for tools no lab or startup would build.

sources.title: Azoulay et al. 2019, Funding breakthrough research, the ARPA model

nodes.name: International big-science laboratories
nodes.summary: Treaty-based labs where many countries pool money for machines none could build alone, starting with CERN in 1954. The model was reused for ITER, the European Southern Observatory and the ISS.

efforts.note: Tim Berners-Lee invented the web there in 1989.

nodes.name: International standards bodies (ISO)
nodes.summary: The International Organization for Standardization, founded in 1947, which sets shared specifications so parts, containers, screws and paperwork work across borders. Its 1968 container standard made global intermodal shipping work.

efforts.note: Electrical, telecom and internet standards bodies.

nodes.name: Venture capital
nodes.summary: Funds that buy stakes in young, risky technology companies and expect most to fail and a few to pay for all, begun by Georges Doriot's American Research and Development in 1946. It funded much of semiconductors, computing, biotech and now space and fusion.

efforts.who: Georges Doriot, American Research and Development Corporation
efforts.note: A $70,000 stake in Digital Equipment (1957) became hundreds of millions.

efforts.who: Arthur Rock; Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia (1972)
efforts.note: The 1979 ERISA prudent-man rule let pension funds invest.

efforts.who: Israel Yozma (1993); China state guidance funds

sources.title: Nicholas, VC, An American History (Harvard University Press)

nodes.name: Outer Space Treaty
nodes.summary: The 1967 UN treaty that declares space free for all to explore, bans claims of national sovereignty and nuclear weapons in orbit, and makes states responsible for their companies' activities. It still frames debates over lunar bases and asteroid mining.

efforts.who: United Nations (US, USSR, UK first signers)

efforts.note: Over 50 signatories by 2025; China and Russia stand apart.

nodes.name: Montreal Protocol
nodes.summary: The 1987 treaty that phased out ozone-destroying CFCs, ratified by every UN member state. The ozone layer is on track to recover by about 2066, making it the most successful global environmental agreement.

efforts.who: Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland (1974); Joe Farman, British Antarctic Survey (1985)
efforts.note: Predicted, then found, the ozone hole.

efforts.who: UNEP and signatories; Kigali Amendment (2016) on HFCs

WMO, Ozone layer on track to recover within four decades (2023)

nodes.name: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
nodes.summary: A UN body, founded in 1988, in which thousands of volunteer scientists assess published climate research and governments approve the summaries line by line. Its reports set the scientific basis for the Paris Agreement.

efforts.who: World Meteorological Organization and UN Environment Programme
efforts.note: Shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize; Sixth Assessment 2021 to 2023, Seventh cycle under way.

nodes.name: Free and open-source software
nodes.summary: Licensing software so anyone may use, study, change and share it, organized around Richard Stallman's GNU project (1983) and the term "open source" (1998). Linux and other open projects now run most servers, phones and cloud infrastructure.

efforts.who: Richard Stallman, GNU project and GPL (1989)
Open Source Initiative (Bruce Perens, Eric Raymond)
GitHub (2008); open-weight AI models (Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen)

nodes.name: Prediction markets and forecasting platforms
nodes.summary: Markets where people bet on future events, so prices act as probabilities, plus scored forecasting communities. From the Iowa Electronic Markets in 1988 to Kalshi and Polymarket, they often beat polls and pundits.

efforts.who: University of Iowa, Iowa Electronic Markets
Robin Hanson (idea futures); DARPA Policy Analysis Market (cancelled 2003)
IARPA ACE tournament, Good Judgment Project (Philip Tetlock); Metaculus (2015)

sources.title: Wolfers and Zitzewitz 2004, Prediction Markets, Journal of Economic Perspectives

nodes.name: Inducement prizes and advance market commitments
nodes.summary: Paying for results instead of effort: a prize for the first to hit a goal, or a promise to buy a product if someone makes it. The Ansari XPRIZE was won by SpaceShipOne in 2004; a 2009 vaccine commitment and the 2022 Frontier carbon removal fund used the buyer's version.

efforts.who: XPRIZE Foundation (Peter Diamandis), Ansari X Prize
efforts.note: Won by Scaled Composites, funded by Paul Allen.
$1.5 billion; vaccines reached low-income countries years faster.

nodes.name: Carbon pricing
nodes.summary: Making emitters pay for CO2, through taxes or capped tradeable permits, so markets find the cheapest cuts. The EU Emissions Trading System began in 2005; about a quarter of world emissions now face some carbon price.

efforts.note: Largest by covered emissions, at low prices.

sources.title: World Bank, State and Trends of Carbon Pricing

nodes.name: Electrolysis
nodes.summary: Splitting compounds with electric current, first done to water weeks after Volta announced his pile. Humphry Davy used it to isolate sodium and potassium in 1807, and Faraday worked out its laws in 1833.

efforts.note: Isolated potassium and sodium.

nodes.name: Chromatography
nodes.summary: Separating a mixture by how fast its parts move through a medium. Mikhail Tsvet separated plant pigments this way in 1903; Martin and Synge's partition chromatography (1941) made it a general laboratory tool.

efforts.note: Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1952.

nodes.name: Synchrotrons and particle colliders
nodes.summary: Accelerators that keep particles in step as they gain energy, then rings that collide two beams head on. They made the particle discoveries behind the Standard Model possible.

efforts.note: Phase stability, the principle behind the synchrotron.
The first hadron collider.

metrics.name: Cost to sequence a human genome
metrics.note: NHGRI Genome Sequencing Program production costs, all 78 data points as published (Sept 2001 to May 2022; page last updated May 16, 2023). Years are fractional: each point is dated to the end of its month (for example 2001.75 is 2001-09-30). Values are in nominal US dollars, rounded to the cent. A 'genome' is 3,000 Mb at the coverage of the era's dominant platform (about 6x Sanger before 2008, about 30x short reads after), and costs include labor, reagents, instrument depreciation, informatics and overhead, but not assembly or analysis. The cliff from late 2007 to 2009 is the switch from capillary Sanger to second-generation sequencers. The May 2022 point repeats the February 2022 value in the source.

metrics.name: Cost per megabase of DNA sequence
metrics.note: NHGRI Genome Sequencing Program production costs, all 78 data points as published (Sept 2001 to May 2022; page last updated May 16, 2023). Years are fractional: each point is dated to the end of its month (for example 2001.75 is 2001-09-30). Values are nominal US dollars per million bases of raw sequence, rounded to six significant figures. Sanger-era data counts Phred Q20 bases; second-generation data uses each platform's own quality threshold. Moore's law (halving every two years) would have taken $5,292 to about $4 by mid-2022; the actual figure is about $0.006, roughly 700 times lower.
